## Initial Full Regression Model

Following the initial data analysis, we construct a multiple linear regression model using daily product demand as the response variable. The initial full model includes nine predictors selected based on their practical relevance to retail product demand.

Price, discount, promotion, and competitor pricing are included to account for any pricing strategies, and market competition. Epidemic and weather conditions are included to capture external factors that may influence consumer purchasing behavior. Region and seasonality are included to account for geographical and seasonal differences in demand. Product category is included to account for differences in demand across different types of products, which was observed in the initial data analysis.

Even though the initial data analysis reveals a strong positive correlation between price and competitive pricing, both variables are retained in the initial model because of their practical relevance. Potential multicollinearity and other model inadequacies will be investigated in subsequent sections.

The initial full regression is estimated using ordinary least squares (OLS) and serves as a baseline for subsequent model diagnostics, and model selection. 

```{r full-fit}
library(broom)
library(knitr)

fit <- lm(demand ~ price + discount + promotion + competitor_pricing + epidemic +
            category + region + seasonality + weather_condition,
          data = dat)
reg_table(fit, caption = "Initial full model: OLS coefficient estimates")
```

The initial full regression model indicates that all individual regression coefficients, except for the coefficient associated with Spring, are statistically significant at the 5% significance level. The corresponding 95% confidence invertals (CIs) exclude zero for all coefficents except Spring. 

The pricing and promotional predictors, price, discount, promotion, and competitor pricing are all positively associated with demand. Holding all other predictors constant, a one-unit increase in price, discount, and competitor pricing is associated with an estimated increase in mean demand of 0.326, 0.302, and 0.073 units, respectively. Promoted products have an estimated mean demand 26.055 units higher than non-promoted products.

There are considerable differences when it comes to product category in demand. Clothing, Electronics, Furniture and Toys have a lower estimated mean demand by 19.691, 60.167, and 2.228 units (respectively) compared to Groceries which has a higher estimated mean demand by 16.089 units -- holding all other predictors constant. These findings are consistent with the differences in demand distribution observed during the initial data analysis. 

With external conditions, epidemic conditions are associated with a decrease of 39.211 units in estimated mean demand. Rainy and snowy weather conditions are negatively associated with demand relative to the reference weather condition; sunny weather is positively associated with demand. Regional and seasonal differences are also observed, yet their estimated magnitudes are generally smaller. 

Price exhibits a positive regression coefficient despite it being a weak negative correlation with demand observed during the initial data analysis. This difference suggests that the association between price and demand changes after accounting for other predictors. Given the strong correlation between price and competitor pricing, potential multicollinearity warrants further investigation in subsequent sections.

Although the initial model identifies several statistically significant associations, further model diagnostics are necessary to assess the validity of the underlying regression assumptions and the reliability of these results.






```{r full-glance}
glance(fit) |>
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, statistic, p.value, AIC, BIC) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, caption = "Initial full model: fit statistics") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

The initial full regression model yields an $R^2$ of 0.442, indicating that approximately 44.2% of the variability in demand is explained by the model. The adjusted $R^2$ is also 0.442, and the residual standard error is 35.097 units.

To evaluate the overall significance of the regression model, we conduct an F-test with the following hypotheses:

$$H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \cdots = \beta_{18} = 0$$

$$H_a: \text{At least one } \beta_j \neq 0$$

The F-statistic is 3339.138 with a p-value less than 0.001. Therefore, we reject $H_0$ and conclude that at least one predictor is significantly associated with demand under the baseline, Gauss-Markov regression assumptions.

Although the overall model is statistically significant, further diagnostics are necessary to assess the underlying regression assumptions and identify potential model inadequacies.
